bigIdea.en: Start the year as a doer of math: explore patterns, share reasoning, and build problem-solving habits.

bigIdea.en: Everyone uses math every day — at home, at school, and in the neighborhood. When a problem feels big, first understand it, then break it into smaller parts and keep trying. A quick estimate or mental math helps you check if your answer makes sense.

bigIdea.en: A statistical question has answers that change from person to person, so you collect data to answer it. A question with only one fixed answer is not a statistical question. For example, "How tall is each student in the class?" is statistical, but "How many days are in a week?" is not.
bigIdea.es: Una pregunta estadística tiene respuestas que cambian de una persona a otra, así que reúnes datos para responderla. Una pregunta con una sola respuesta fija no es estadística. Por ejemplo, «¿Cuánto mide cada estudiante de la clase?» es estadística, pero «¿Cuántos días tiene una semana?» no lo es.

teacher.objective: I can tell the difference between a statistical question and a non-statistical question.
misconceptions: A common mistake in Statistical Questions and Data is judging a question by its topic or its numbers instead of its variability. Students see a question about ONE player, ONE game, or ONE fixed fact — like "How many points does the team need to win a game?" — and call it statistical just because it has a number or is about sports. Or they see a question about a single player's whole season, like "How many touchdowns did the quarterback throw this season?", and call it NOT statistical because only one player is named, forgetting that a season covers many games with a different result each time. Both errors skip the real test: will the answers actually differ from case to case (game to game, player to player)? If yes, it is a statistical question; if there is one fixed answer, it is not.

title.en: Describe the Data Using the Median

bigIdea.en: The median is the middle number after you put the numbers in order from least to greatest. If there are two middle numbers, the median is the number exactly halfway between them.
bigIdea.es: La mediana es el número del medio después de ordenar los números de menor a mayor. Si hay dos números en el medio, la mediana es el número que está exactamente a la mitad entre ellos.

teacher.objective: I can find the median of a data set and use it to describe what is typical.
misconceptions: A common mistake in Mean, Median, and Mode is finding the median without ordering the data first — students pick the middle number straight from the list as given (for 9, 4, 7, 2, 6 they say the median is 7, the middle position in that original order) instead of sorting least to greatest (2, 4, 6, 7, 9) and finding the true middle value, 6. title.en: Represent and Describe Data in a Box Plot
title.es: Representar y describir datos en un diagrama de caja

bigIdea.en: A box plot shows how data is spread out using five numbers: the lowest, the first quartile (Q1), the median, the third quartile (Q3), and the highest. The box goes from Q1 to Q3 and holds the middle half of the data; its length is Q3 − Q1. Lines called whiskers reach from the box out to the lowest and highest numbers.
bigIdea.es: Un diagrama de caja muestra cómo se reparten los datos usando cinco números: el menor, el primer cuartil (Q1), la mediana, el tercer cuartil (Q3) y el mayor. La caja va de Q1 a Q3 y contiene la mitad central de los datos; su largo es Q3 − Q1. Unas líneas llamadas bigotes van desde la caja hasta el número menor y el número mayor.

sentenceFrames: The model shows ___ so the answer is ___.

teacher.objective: I can make and read a box plot to summarize a data set.
misconceptions: A common mistake in Display Data: Box Plots is treating a quartile as just one data point instead of the median of a half — for the lower half 4, 8, 10, 14, some students pick 10 (the last value) as Q1 instead of finding the median of that half: Q1 = (8 + 10) ÷ 2 = 9. A second common slip is finding IQR by adding the quartiles instead of subtracting, writing IQR = Q3 + Q1 (like 30 + 18 = 48) instead of IQR = Q3 − Q1 (30 − 18 = 12) — always order the data first, then subtract Q1 from Q3 to find the spread of the middle 50%.

title.en: Describe Data by Range and Interquartile Range
title.es: Describir datos con el rango y el rango intercuartílico

bigIdea.en: The range tells how spread out all of the data is: range = greatest number − least number. The interquartile range (IQR) tells how spread out the middle half of the data is: IQR = Q3 − Q1.
bigIdea.es: El rango dice qué tan separados están todos los datos: rango = número mayor − número menor. El rango intercuartílico dice qué tan separada está la mitad central de los datos: rango intercuartílico = Q3 − Q1.

sentenceFrames: The model shows ___ so the answer is ___.

teacher.objective: I can find the range and the interquartile range of a data set and use them to describe how spread out the data is.
misconceptions: A common mistake with Range and Interquartile Range is adding the two quartiles instead of subtracting them — writing IQR = Q3 + Q1. With Q1 = 42 and Q3 = 58 that gives 100, which is larger than the data set's entire range of 20. Every measure of variation is a DIFFERENCE, and the IQR can never exceed the range, because the middle half is part of the whole span. If your IQR comes out bigger than your range, you added when you should have subtracted.

title.en: Divide Multi-Digit Numbers Using an Algorithm
title.es: Dividir números de varias cifras con un algoritmo

bigIdea.en: Long division splits a number into equal groups, one digit at a time. Repeat four steps — divide, multiply, subtract, bring down — until there are no digits left. Anything left over at the end is the remainder.
bigIdea.es: La división larga reparte un número en grupos iguales, un dígito a la vez. Repite cuatro pasos — divide, multiplica, resta, baja — hasta que no queden dígitos. Lo que sobre al final es el residuo.

sentenceFrames: The model shows ___ so the answer is ___.

teacher.objective: I can divide multi-digit whole numbers and explain the meaning of the quotient and remainder.
misconceptions: A common mistake in Divide Multi-Digit Numbers is skipping a placeholder zero in the quotient when a digit doesn't divide evenly, which shifts every digit after it out of place. For example, dividing 3,216 ÷ 3: 3 ÷ 3 = 1, but the next digit 2 doesn't divide by 3, so a 0 must be written before continuing — bring down the 1 to make 21 ÷ 3 = 7, then bring down 6 ÷ 3 = 2, giving the correct quotient 1,072. A student who skips writing that 0 and jumps straight to 21 ÷ 3 = 7 ends up with 172 instead of 1,072 — an answer off by a factor of ten. title.en: Describe Data by Mean Absolute Deviation

bigIdea.en: The mean absolute deviation (MAD) tells how spread out the data is. Find the mean, find how far each number is from the mean, then find the average of those distances. A small MAD means the numbers are close together; a large MAD means they are spread out.
bigIdea.es: La desviación media absoluta dice qué tan separados están los datos. Halla la media, halla qué tan lejos está cada número de la media y luego halla el promedio de esas distancias. teacher.objective: I can find the mean absolute deviation (MAD) to describe how spread out data is.
misconceptions: A common mistake in Mean Absolute Deviation is adding the signed deviations (value − mean) instead of their absolute values, so the positives and negatives cancel out to 0. For 6, 8, 10, 12 (mean = 9), the deviations are −3, −1, 1, 3 — they sum to 0, but that is NOT the MAD. Before averaging, take the absolute value of every deviation so each becomes a nonnegative distance, including zero: |−3| = 3, |−1| = 1, |1| = 1, |3| = 3. Sum = 8, so MAD = 8 ÷ 4 = 2. A MAD of exactly 0 is a warning sign — it only happens if every value in the data set equals the mean.

misconceptions: A common mistake with percent is scaling only one term of the ratio: reading 7 out of 10 as 7%. A percent compares to 100, so BOTH terms must be multiplied by the same factor — 10 × 10 = 100, so 7 × 10 = 70, giving 70%. misconceptions: A common mistake in Relate Fractions, Decimals, and Percents is treating the numerator and denominator as the percent's digits — turning 3/5 into "35%" by just reading the 3 and the 5. Percent means out of 100, so the fix is to build an equivalent fraction with denominator 100: 5 × 20 = 100, so multiply the top by 20 too — 3/5 = 60/100 = 60%. A second version of this mistake is scaling only ONE part of the fraction (writing 3/5 = 3/100 or 60/5). Whatever you multiply the denominator by, you must multiply the numerator by the same number. When a denominator will not reach 100 evenly (8, 3, 7), divide the numerator by the denominator instead and then multiply by 100.

teacher.objective: I can determine the whole when I know a part and the percent that part represents.

title.en: Determine the Area of Parallelograms and Rhombuses

bigIdea.en: To find the area of a parallelogram, multiply the base by the height. The height goes straight up from the base, not along the slanted side. Example: a base of 6 ft and a height of 4 ft gives 6 × 4 = 24 square feet.

bigIdea.en: The least common multiple (LCM) is the smallest number that two numbers both count up to. Count by 4s: 4, 8, 12. Count by 6s: 6, 12. The first number on both lists is 12, so the LCM of 4 and 6 is 12.

teacher.objective: I can find the least common multiple (LCM) of two numbers by listing or comparing their multiples.
misconceptions: A common mistake in Least Common Multiple is multiplying the two numbers together instead of listing multiples to find the smallest shared one. For example, for 4 and 6, a student calculates 4 × 6 = 24 and calls that the LCM, but the actual least common multiple is 12 (multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12; multiples of 6: 6, 12 — 12 is the first number that appears in both lists). This shortcut only works when the two numbers share no common factors (like 4 and 9, where the LCM really is 36 = 4 × 9); for numbers like 4 and 6 that share a factor of 2, multiplying overshoots the true LCM. Always list multiples of both numbers and pick the first one that appears in both lists.

bigIdea.en: Integers are the counting numbers (1, 2, 3, ...), their opposites (-1, -2, -3, ...), and 0. Opposites are the same distance from 0 on different sides, like 5 and -5. Zero often means a starting point, like sea level or $0 in a bank account.

title.es: Comprender el valor absoluto de números racionales

bigIdea.en: The absolute value of a number is how far it is from 0 on the number line. Distance is never negative, so |-7| = 7 and |7| = 7. This works for fractions and decimals too: |-2.5| = 2.5.
bigIdea.es: El valor absoluto de un número es qué tan lejos está del 0 en la recta numérica. Una distancia nunca es negativa, así que |-7| = 7 y |7| = 7. También sirve para fracciones y decimales: |-2.5| = 2.5.

teacher.objective: I can find the absolute value of a rational number — an integer, fraction, or decimal — as its distance from zero.
misconceptions: A common mistake in Integers and Absolute Value is judging size by the digits alone instead of position on the number line — students think -8 is 'more' than -3 because 8 > 3, when really -8 sits farther left (colder, deeper, or lower) and is actually the SMALLER integer. Absolute value measures distance from zero and is always positive or zero, but that distance does not decide which integer is greater — only left-to-right order on the number line does. Before you submit, ask: am I comparing distance from zero (absolute value) or position on the number line (greater/less than)?

title.en: Compare and Order Integers and Rational Numbers

bigIdea.en: On a number line, numbers get bigger as you go right and smaller as you go left. So -10 is less than -2, because -10 is farther left. To put numbers in order, picture where each one sits on the line.

It's the opposite for negatives: the number farther to the left on the number line (farther from zero) is always the LESSER value, so -15 < -8. Before you submit, check your comparison against the number line, not just the digits.

title.en: Represent Rational Numbers on the Coordinate Plane
title.es: Representar números racionales en el plano de coordenadas

bigIdea.en: A point on a graph is named by two numbers in parentheses, like (3, -2). Start at (0, 0). The first number tells how far to move right (positive) or left (negative). The second number tells how far to move up (positive) or down (negative).
bigIdea.es: Un punto en una gráfica se nombra con dos números entre paréntesis, como (3, -2). Empieza en (0, 0). El primer número dice cuánto moverse a la derecha (positivo) o a la izquierda (negativo). El segundo número dice cuánto moverse hacia arriba (positivo) o hacia abajo (negativo).

title.en: Determine Distance on the Coordinate Plane
title.es: Determinar distancias en el plano de coordenadas

bigIdea.en: When two points are in the same row or the same column on a graph, you can find how far apart they are from their numbers. For (2, -3) and (2, 4), count from -3 up to 4: that is 7 units. Distance is never negative.
bigIdea.es: Cuando dos puntos están en la misma fila o en la misma columna de una gráfica, puedes saber qué tan separados están usando sus números. Para (2, -3) y (2, 4), cuenta de -3 hasta 4: son 7 unidades. Una distancia nunca es negativa.

teacher.objective: I can find the distance between two points on the coordinate plane using absolute value.
misconceptions: A common mistake in Distance on the Coordinate Plane is subtracting the coordinates as if both points were on the same side of zero, instead of adding their absolute values when the points are on opposite sides. For example, to find the distance between (-6, 3) and (2, 3), a student might subtract 6 − 2 = 4, but since -6 and 2 are on opposite sides of zero, the absolute values must be added instead: |-6| + |2| = 6 + 2 = 8. The correct distance is 8 units, not 4. Before you submit, ask: 'Are these two points on opposite sides of zero — and if so, did I add the absolute values instead of subtracting?'

bigIdea.en: You can draw a shape on a graph by plotting its corner points and connecting them in order. The corner numbers also tell you how long each side is. For example, from (-2, 3) to (4, 3) is 6 units. Add all the sides to get the perimeter.

title.en: Ordered Pairs in All Four Quadrants
title.es: Pares ordenados en los cuatro cuadrantes

bigIdea.en: A graph has four parts called quadrants. The signs of a point's two numbers tell which part it is in. A negative first number means move left, and a negative second number means move down. For example, (-4, 3) is in the upper-left part, Quadrant II.
bigIdea.es: Una gráfica tiene cuatro partes llamadas cuadrantes. Los signos de los dos números de un punto dicen en qué parte está. Si el primer número es negativo, te mueves a la izquierda; si el segundo número es negativo, te mueves hacia abajo. Por ejemplo, (-4, 3) está en la parte de arriba a la izquierda, el Cuadrante II.

title.es: Reflejar puntos respecto a los ejes

bigIdea.en: Reflecting a point is like flipping it over a mirror line. Flip over the x-axis and only the second number changes sign: (2, 5) becomes (2, -5). Flip over the y-axis and only the first number changes sign: (2, 5) becomes (-2, 5).

title.es: Comprender las ecuaciones y sus soluciones

bigIdea.en: An equation is a math sentence that says two sides are equal, like n + 3 = 8. A solution is a number that makes the equation true. To check, put the number in place of the letter: 5 + 3 = 8, so 5 is the solution.
bigIdea.es: Una ecuación es una oración matemática que dice que dos lados son iguales, como n + 3 = 8. Una solución es un número que hace verdadera la ecuación. Para comprobar, pon el número en lugar de la letra: 5 + 3 = 8, así que 5 es la solución.

teacher.objective: I can write an equation for a real situation and check whether a given value is a solution by substituting it.
misconceptions: A common mistake in Write Equations is writing subtraction and division clues in the wrong order — putting the number from the clue first instead of the variable first. For 'a number decreased by 8 equals 5,' students often write 8 − n = 5 instead of the correct n − 8 = 5; for 'a number divided by 4 equals 6,' they write 4 ÷ n (or 4n) instead of n / 4 = 6. Always start with the variable, then attach the operation in the order the words describe it, and check by substituting your answer back in.

bigIdea.en: An inequality shows that many numbers can work, not just one. "At least 12" means 12 or more, so we write n ≥ 12. "At most 10" means 10 or less, so we write n ≤ 10.

teacher.objective: I can write inequalities to represent real-world situations.
misconceptions: A common mistake in Write Inequalities is using a strict symbol (> or <) for a phrase that actually includes the boundary value. For 'the suspect is at least 18 years old,' students often write a > 18 instead of the correct a ≥ 18 — this wrongly excludes 18 itself, even though 'at least 18' means 18 counts as a match. The same error happens in reverse with 'at most': for 'the getaway bag holds at most 12 items,' students write n < 12 instead of n ≤ 12. Always ask: does the key phrase include the number ('at least,' 'at most,' 'no more than,' 'no fewer than' → use ≥ or ≤) or exclude it ('more than,' 'fewer than' → use > or <)?

title.es: Comprender las desigualdades y sus soluciones

bigIdea.en: The answers to an inequality can be shown on a number line: put a circle at the boundary number and shade the side that works. An open circle means that number is not included (< or >), and a filled-in circle means it is included (≤ or ≥). For x ≥ 4, fill in the circle at 4 and shade to the right.

Un círculo abierto quiere decir que ese número no está incluido (< o >), y un círculo relleno quiere decir que sí está incluido (≤ o ≥). Para x ≥ 4, rellena el círculo en 4 y sombrea hacia la derecha.

teacher.objective: I can graph the solutions of an inequality on a number line.

A second common mistake is choosing the right circle but shading the wrong direction — for x < 9 students sometimes shade right instead of left. Always check the symbol twice: once for the circle (does it have an 'or equal to' line?) and once for the shading direction (does the symbol point toward larger or smaller numbers?).

teacher.objective: I can solve an inequality and graph its solution set on a number line.
misconceptions: A common mistake in Solve and Graph Inequalities is shading the number line in the wrong direction after solving. For example, a student solves x + 4 > 10 correctly to get x > 6, but then shades LEFT toward smaller numbers instead of RIGHT toward greater numbers. The shading direction always matches the solved symbol, not the original problem: '>' and '≥' shade right (greater numbers), '<' and '≤' shade left (smaller numbers) — check this AFTER you solve, not before. To catch this mistake, substitute one shaded value and one unshaded value back into the original inequality: the shaded value should make it true, and the unshaded value should make it false.

bigIdea.en: Turn a real story into math: use an equation (=) when there is one exact answer, and an inequality (<, >, ≤, ≥) when there is a limit like "at least" or "at most." Then solve it and check that the answer makes sense in the story.

teacher.objective: I can model and solve real-world problems using equations and inequalities.
misconceptions: A common mistake in Equations and Inequalities Problem Solving is matching the wrong model to a key phrase. For 'the getaway car held no more than 6 bags,' students often write the equation b = 6 instead of the inequality b ≤ 6, because they see one number and assume it must be exact. The same mistake happens in reverse: for 'the reward split equally among 5 people gave each $40,' students sometimes write the inequality 5p ≥ 40 instead of the equation 5p = 40, because 'split equally' sounds like it could mean a range. Before you submit, ask: does this phrase give one exact value (equation, =) or a limit/range (inequality, <, >, ≤, ≥)?

bigIdea.en: When two amounts change together, one depends on the other. The amount you choose or change is the independent variable, and the amount that responds is the dependent variable. title.en: Analyze Graphs of Relationships Between Two Variables

bigIdea.en: A table and a graph can show the same relationship. Each row of the table, like (2, 10), becomes a point on the graph: go 2 across and 10 up. The independent variable goes on the bottom (across) axis, and the dependent variable goes on the side (up) axis.
